name: Ananthapura Lake Temple
tagline: Kerala's only lake temple — a serene Vishnu shrine with a famed resident crocodile
summary: Ananthapura Lake Temple is a 9th‑century Vishnu shrine set on a spring‑fed tank in Kasaragod. The footbridge, wood carvings and the temple’s crocodile make it a memorable winter visit.
description: Ananthapura Lake Temple is a small stone shrine built at the centre of a rectangular, spring‑fed lake in Ananthapura village, Manjeshwaram taluk, Kasaragod. It is traditionally regarded as the moolasthanam (original seat) of Lord Ananthapadmanabha.

The site matters for both its unusual siting — reached by a single footbridge — and its layered history and legends (including a cave‑spring said to link it to Padmanabhaswamy in Thiruvananthapuram). The mandapam and the wood‑carved ceilings are fine examples of local temple craft.

For visitors the lake’s stillness, the low stone shrine, the footbridge approach and the temple lore create a contemplative atmosphere. The temple is also famous for a long tradition of a resident crocodile in the tank; the animal figures in local stories and draws curious pilgrims and travellers.
highlights: Only temple in Kerala built in the middle of a lake (spring‑fed rectangular tank).
Considered the moolasthanam of Ananthapadmanabha (Padmanabhaswamy tradition).
Single footbridge approach, namaskara mandapam and intricate wooden ceiling carvings.
Long tradition of a resident temple crocodile (well documented in recent years).
Peaceful setting — especially pleasant and photogenic in winter months.

sections.heading: Background
body: Local tradition places the temple in the early medieval period; its ritual role and legends link it to Vilwamangalam and the origin story of Padmanabhaswamy at Thiruvananthapuram. Ruins around the lake suggest a once larger complex.

Architecturally the temple is compact: a sreekovil (sanctum), namaskara mandapam connected by a footbridge and ancillary shrines. The idol was originally made from a traditional medicinal paste and was replaced by a panchaloha murti in the 20th century; efforts to reinstate older forms have been reported.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Cross the narrow footbridge and pause at the namaskara mandapam for photos of the shrine mirrored in the tank. Look up at the carved wooden ceilings and painted panels in the mandapam depicting Dashavatara scenes.

Listen to the temple stories from the pujari or local guides — the cave‑spring, the ‘original seat’ legend and the crocodile lore are central to the site’s identity. Birdlife and the calm waters make the place good for quiet nature watching.
Observe temple etiquette: stay on designated paths, do not disturb the water or wildlife and follow the pujari’s instructions if you encounter the lake’s resident crocodile.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: The site is small and typically a short visit (30–60 minutes) fits well into a Kasaragod/Bekal day trip. There are no reliable public displays of fixed opening hours online — confirm darshan times with the temple committee or local tourist office before you travel.

Nearest train access is Kumbla railway station (about 4–6 km); Kasaragod town and Bekal are convenient bases for road access. The lake setting is at its most pleasant in the cool, dry winter months when light and visibility are best for photographs.

latest.text: A new crocodile was spotted in the temple lake and the temple authorities held a naming ceremony, naming the newcomer 'Babiya' to commemorate the long‑time resident that died in 2022.
The long‑time resident crocodile 'Babiya' was found dead on October 9, 2022; its death drew large public attention and funeral rites at the temple.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Winter (November–February) — cool, dry weather and clear light make the lake and shrine especially pleasant.
visitorInfo.howToReach: By road from Kasaragod or Kumbla; nearest railhead Kumbla (about 4–6 km). Nearest airport: Mangalore (approx. 54 km by road). Local buses and taxis connect from Kasaragod/Kumbla; confirm local transport and temple timings before travel.
etiquette: Confirm darshan/visiting times with the temple committee or Kasaragod tourist office before you go.
Do not feed or disturb the crocodile or other wildlife — follow temple staff directions for safety.
Wear modest clothing and remove shoes where required; photography may be restricted during rituals.
Carry sun protection and water in summer; winter mornings are cool and comfortable for a visit.
